report:
## Conclusion

The best available evidence indicates that saw palmetto (Serenoa repens) preparations do **not** provide meaningful, longer-term symptom relief for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) compared with placebo.

The most authoritative source is the updated Cochrane systematic review (2023), which pooled multiple placebo-controlled randomized trials and concluded that Serenoa repens monotherapy provides "little to no benefit" for lower urinary tract symptoms due to BPH, with only low-to-moderate certainty evidence and no clinically meaningful improvement in IPSS scores or urinary flow measures versus placebo (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD001423_serenoa-repens-benign-prostatic-hyperplasia; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37345871/).

This aligns with the large, rigorously designed CAMUS (Complementary and Alternative Medicine for Urologic Symptoms) trial, a multi-year, dose-escalation, placebo-controlled study published in the New England Journal of Medicine. Even when saw palmetto doses were increased up to three times the standard dose (320mg to 960mg/day) over 72 weeks, there was no significant improvement in urinary symptom scores compared to placebo (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3979451/).

The U.S. National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH), a government authority, similarly summarizes that "a large study evaluating high doses of saw palmetto and a Cochrane review found that saw palmetto was not more effective than placebo for treatment of urinary symptoms related to BPH" (https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/providers/digest/spotlight-on-saw-palmetto-science).

Some combination formulations with other phytotherapeutic agents showed statistically significant but modest improvement in short-term trials (12–24 weeks), but evidence for long-term efficacy remains uncertain and of lower quality.

**Bottom line:** Based on high-quality, long-term randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews, saw palmetto alone does not meaningfully improve BPH symptoms over placebo, even at higher doses over extended periods. Saw palmetto is generally considered safe, but current evidence does not support its use as an effective treatment for BPH symptoms.
